variants.name: Protocol-based passive view (UIKit)
variants.idiom_name: protocol View: AnyObject + presenter class with a weak view reference; view controller conforms
variants.implementation_notes: The classic iOS shape: a class-bound protocol declares the screen's semantic operations, the UIViewController or a custom UIView conforms, and the presenter is a plain class (no UIKit import) taking the protocol plus the model. Gestures are forwarded by the view controller; the presenter pushes updates back through the protocol, and tests substitute a protocol-conforming double. ARC handles most lifetime issues, but the view reference should be weak/unowned so the screen can be released, and protocol extensions can supply default implementations for members the presenter may ignore. Use this form for UIKit code bases; SwiftUI replaces it with observable state-driven views rather than presenters.
pitfalls: A weak optional view quietly swallows updates after deallocation; log or assert on a nil view so a released screen is visible instead of silently dead.
Strong view<->presenter references form a retain cycle; keep the presenter's view reference weak/unowned and clear it in viewDidDisappear/dismantle.
UIKit is main-thread-only: presenter work finishing on a background queue must hop back via DispatchQueue.main.async before touching the view.

variants.name: Closure-callback view contract
variants.idiom_name: view exposes closure properties (onQueryChanged, showTotal) assigned by the presenter/host
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of protocol methods, the view can publish its contract as closure properties - showTotal: (Double) -> Void, onQueryChanged: (String) -> Void - which the presenter (or the assembly code) assigns, with [weak self] captures where needed. This suits small screens or view types that must not know about a protocol, and it maps naturally onto UIKit target-action or SwiftUI closures. Prefer the protocol form once the contract grows or several view implementations must be substituted by type, since closures erase the contract's shape and Swift gives no compiler check that all callbacks were assigned.
pitfalls: Optional closures fail silently when unassigned; assign every callback at wiring time or make the view's initializer require them.
Closures capturing the presenter/view strongly create retain cycles; use [weak self]/[weak presenter] when the capture outlives the call.
Closure-based contracts cannot be exhaustively checked; a protocol is safer once more than a couple of callbacks exist.
